::: {.solutions}

**20 questions.** Suggested time: **85 minutes**, no calculator.

Every question comes from a TMUA past paper, a TMUA mock paper, the MAT or the official Notes on Logic and Proof, and its
source is shown beside the question number. None of them appears in the S5 class questions.

For every question the routine is the same: **write the claim as "if … then", then ask whether each candidate satisfies the
hypothesis and whether it breaks the conclusion.** To decide a "must be true" statement, either prove it for every case or
find one case that breaks it.

| Section | What it covers | Questions |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Which candidates work?** | hold each candidate against the hypothesis first, then the conclusion | 1–8 |
| **B — Prove it or break it** | deciding whether a claim always holds, then proving it or finding one failure | 9–17 |
| **C — Judging a proof** | finding where a direct proof or a proof by contradiction goes wrong | 18–20 |

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA early specimen · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
A set of five cards each have a letter printed on their front and a number printed on their back, as follows:

| | Card A | Card B | Card C | Card D | Card E |
|---|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| **Fronts** | A | B | C | D | E |
| **Backs** | 3 | 4 | 1 | 7 | 8 |

Which one of the five cards (A, B, C, D or E) provides a **counterexample** to the following statement?

> *Every card that has a vowel on its front has an even number on its back.*
:::

The fact above can be used to provide a counterexample to which of these statements?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** 1 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** 2 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** 1, 2 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** 1, 3 and 4 only

::: {.question}

Given two linear polynomials, we define an operation $\cdot$ as follows. To calculate $f(x)\cdot g(x)$, we multiply the
polynomials as normal, but we ignore any $x^2$ term.

For example, $(1-2x)\cdot(3-5x)=3-11x$, because we are ignoring the $10x^2$ term.

A strictly increasing linear function $f(x)$ has the property that if $y>x$ then $f(y)>f(x)$.

A student claims that if $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are both strictly increasing linear functions then so is $f(x)\cdot g(x)$. Is
the student correct? If so, prove the student's claim. Otherwise, find a counterexample.
:::

## Question 19 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q5</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to prove the following claim:

> For every positive integer $n$, if $n^2+2$ is prime, then $n$ is a multiple of $3$.

The student's argument is given line by line below.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I.** Suppose $n$ is a positive integer such that $n^2+2$ is prime, but $n$ is not a multiple of $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II.** Then the remainder of $n$ on division by $3$ is $1$ or $2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III.** In either case, $n^2$ leaves remainder $1$ when divided by $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV.** Therefore $n^2+2$ leaves remainder $0$ when divided by $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**V.** So $3$ divides $n^2+2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VI.** Hence $n^2+2=3k$ for some integer $k$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VII.** It follows that $n^2+2$ is composite and not prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VIII.** This contradicts the assumption in (I) that $n^2+2$ is prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IX.** Therefore $n$ is a multiple of $3$.

Which one of the following statements about the argument is correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The argument is completely correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The first error in the argument is on line I.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The first error in the argument is on line II.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The first error in the argument is on line III.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The first error in the argument is on line IV.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** The first error in the argument is on line V.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** The first error in the argument is on line VI.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** The first error in the argument is on line VII.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** The first error in the argument is on line VIII.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**J** The first error in the argument is on line IX.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:6cm"}
Working
:::

## Question 20 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">JZ Maths Mock A · P2 Q17</span>

::: {.question}
In this question, $n$ is an integer greater than $1$.

**Statement:** If $n$ does not divide $k!$ for any positive integer $k$ with $k<n$, then $n$ is prime.

The following is an attempted proof of the statement:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(1)** Assume $n$ does not divide $k!$ for any positive integer $k$ with $k<n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(2)** Suppose for contradiction that $n$ is composite, so $n=ab$ for some integers $a,b$ with $1<a\le b<n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(3)** Case 1: $a<b$. Then $a$ and $b$ are distinct integers, each in the set $\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(4)** Therefore $a$ and $b$ both appear as factors in the product $(n-1)!=1\cdot2\cdots(n-1)$, so $ab=n$ divides $(n-1)!$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(5)** Case 2: $a=b$, so $n=a^2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(6)** Since $a\ge2$, the integers $a$ and $2a$ both satisfy $a\ge2$ and $2a\ge4$, so they are positive integers.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(7)** Since $a\ge2$, we have $a<a^2=n$ and $2a<a^2=n$, so $a$ and $2a$ are distinct integers in the set $\{2,3,\dots,n-1\}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(8)** Therefore $a$ and $2a$ both appear as factors in $(n-1)!$, so $a\cdot2a=2a^2=2n$ divides $(n-1)!$, and in particular $n$ divides $(n-1)!$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(9)** In both cases $n$ divides $(n-1)!$, contradicting the assumption in line 1. Hence $n$ is prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** First mistake appears in line 1 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** First mistake appears in line 2 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** First mistake appears in line 3 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** First mistake appears in line 4 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** First mistake appears in line 5 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** First mistake appears in line 6 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** First mistake appears in line 7 and the statement is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** The proof is valid and the statement is true.
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::
